newsitem.title: USA: General Mills to raise cereal prices.
newsitem.headline: General Mills to raise cereal prices.

text.p: General Mills Corp., the nation's second largest cereal maker, said Wednesday it plans to increase prices an average of 2.6 percent, becoming the first major U.S. cereal maker to raise prices since a round of price cuts by the industry a year ago.

The maker of Cheerios, Lucky Charms and many other brands said the price increases, effective immediately, were intended to adjust for inflation and were the first the Minneapolis-based company has made in four years.
The move caught some analysts by surprise, while General Mills' competitors did not say if they would follow suit.

"I think it's probably a surprise to everybody and to my way of thinking is a positive move," said Robert Cummins, a food industry analyst with Schroder & Co. "The net result is the price reductions themselves (last year) had no beneficial effect at all on total consumption."

The increase was the first by a major cereal company since competitor Post Cereal, a division of Philip Morris Cos. Inc.'s Kraft Foods Inc. unit, shook up the $9 billion ready-to-eat cereal industry by cutting prices 20 percent, analysts said.
General Mills, Quaker Oats Co. and industry leader Kellogg Co. followed that move to some extent. Analysts said the price cuts failed to bring more consumers into the cereal aisles.

General Mills said in June that industry-wide the U.S. ready-to-eat cereal category grew by 1 percent in all outlets in its fiscal year 1997, ended May 31. Historically, the category has grown at a 3 percent pace.
The move could be dangerous for General Mills if other cereal makers do not join the price increases, one analyst said.

"It seems to me that General Mills will put itself in a position where if nobody else increases prices along with them, they will be vulnerable to losing some market share," Chris Jakubik, industry analyst at SBC Warburg, said.
A Kellogg spokesman said the company would not comment on future business plans.
"We have said and continue to be optimistic about the long-term growth of the business," said Anthony Hebron, spokesman for Kellogg Co. He added that Kellogg has not increased prices since 1994.
A Quaker Oats spokesman said the company would "watch the category."
Post officials were not immediately available to comment.
Schroder's Cummins said he does not expect across-the-board increases by other cereal companies, but that some scattered increases could follow the move by General Mills.
"I wouldn't be at all surprised to see Kellogg's and some of the others take some selective increases," he said.

He also said it was typical among food companies, after raising prices, to put some of the increase back into marketing. The cereal companies cut back marketing and promotion after cutting prices last year.
In a statement Wednesday, General Mills said that over the past four years the prices of key components of the cereal company's cost structure have increased an average of 12 percent.
General Mills said the new prices remain lower than they were four years ago.
General Mills stock closed up 12.5 cents at $65.75 in consolidated trading Wednesday on the New York Stock Exchange.
